transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Jensen Wong, former head of the chipmaker NVIDIA,
is breaking his silence after stepping down
amid reports he had an affair with a woman
who may have been spying for China.
Wong says he would return a CEO if the board asked,
"Here's NPR's John Ruich."
In a message on X,
Wong said he has seen an outpouring of calls for him
to return since he resigned last week.
Wong has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife,
and reports from the New York Times and others
said he had a relationship with a Chinese woman
who U.S. intelligence agencies suspect
was recruited by Beijing to spy on him.
An online petition to reinstate Wong
has gathered nearly 200,000 names,
including thousands of NVIDIA employees.
Wong now says he'd be honored to come back
if NVIDIA's board decides it's in the best interests
of the company, its shareholders, employees,
and the country.
John Ruich, NPR News.
President Trump's 48-hour trip to Asia
began with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations
Conference in Manila, Philippines.
But by the time he landed,
the summit's closing ceremony was underway.
Trump met with members of a so-called quad
made up of the U.S., India, Japan, and Australia.
He also signed a memorandum of understanding
with Thailand on a trade deal
expected to be finalized in the near future.
But all eyes are on Trump's next stop,
China, host of the APEC Summit.
In Shenzhen, Trump will take part in a trilateral meeting
with his hosts, President Xi Jinping,
and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump has said he'll discuss the war in Ukraine.
Trump has also again floated the possibility
of meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
We have more from NPR's Deepa Shivaram.
-This is going to be a pretty historic meeting.
These three leaders have never met together.
-Trump has been saying for a while now
that he wants to discuss denuclearization
with Xi and Putin, but I will say it's not really a topic
that China is keen to get into.
Trump has also said he wants to discuss with them,
you know, about the war in Iran.
-NPR's Deepa Shivaram.
It's looking as though Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
will not take part in a White House hearing next month.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports a hearing is supposedly designed
to weigh allegations that Cook committed mortgage fraud.
-The White House announced the hearing
after the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year
that President Trump could not fire Lisa Cook
without a measure of due process.
But in a letter this week,
Cook's attorney argues the proposed hearing
offers only a facade of due process.
The letter says Cook has no obligation
to participate in an unfair hearing
and, in fact, has a duty to avoid any process
that could undermine the central bank's independence.
The standoff likely sets the stage for further litigation,
but even if Trump were able to remove Cook
from the Fed's governing board, he's likely to have
a tough-time-winning confirmation for any replacement
once Democrats take control of the incoming Senate.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
-You're listening to NPR News.
After 26 years of progress,
the U.S. has lost its measles-eliminated status.
The Pan American Health Organization
formally announced its decision today
as the U.S. battles a surge in measles cases
and a decline in vaccination rates among children.
The outbreaks in North America began in Mennonite communities
and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates.
Mexico has also lost its measles-free designation.
Canada did so last year for the first time since 1998.
Does locking up students' cell phones at school
lead to better test scores in math and reading?
NPR's Corey Turner reports on a new study that suggests yes.
In the U.S., student test scores began a long slide around 2013,
about the same time teens were getting their hands on smartphones.
So, in this new study, researchers from Harvard
and Dartmouth looked specifically at schools
that adopted cell phone pouches,
where kids kept their phones locked away all day.
And then they compared those students to schools
without strict phone bans.
They found students in the pouch schools
did get a small boost in achievement,
equivalent to what they might learn with one to two extra weeks of school.
A previous study, though, found a close-to-zero effect on test scores.
So, these new findings have researchers hopeful,
while also saying there's a lot more research to be done.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
-NFA official requesting anonymity
because they're not authorized to speak publicly tells NPR.
The agency has paused the installation of Juniper routers,
a kind that played a role in last week's national air ground stop.
It's NPR.
-Wanna hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now,
sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism
and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

Trump's Asia trip begins with ASEAN summit in Manila, quad meeting, Thailand trade memorandum
Trump to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen at APEC, discuss Ukraine
Lisa Cook likely to skip White House mortgage fraud hearing, citing lack of due process
U.S. loses measles-eliminated status as Pan American Health Organization announces decision
Study finds locking students' phones in pouches gives small boost to math and reading scores
FAA pauses installation of Juniper routers after last week's nationwide air ground stop
